idiom_name: token enum + one static function per rule over a shared cursor (Lua lparser.c shape)
implementation_notes: C has no parser library and no exceptions, so the classic structure is written out in full: a token enum, a lexer state struct carrying the current token and its position, one static function per rule, and small helpers that consume conditionally or fail - Lua's lparser.c is the canonical example, with its prototypes for recursive non-terminal functions (statement, expr) and its testnext/check/checknext/error_expected helpers. What replaces the OO structure is file-scope convention: recursion is plain function calls and the grammar's shape is visible as the prototypes. Errors are an error callback plus longjmp, or a per-rule status return that every caller must propagate. Keep the hand-written form - no generated tables - when the grammar is small and you want the parser to be dependency-free, reviewable and portable to freestanding environments; use bison/flex when the grammar grows past a few hundred lines.
pitfalls: Error handling is manual: without setjmp/longjmp or an aborting error callback, every rule must return and propagate a status flag, and one missed check turns a syntax error into a crash on a null node.

Recursion depth is bounded by the C stack (typically a few megabytes) and stack exhaustion is undefined behaviour, not an exception: a depth counter must reject deeply nested input before the limit is reached.
Token payloads must outlive the parse: string views into a mutable input buffer dangle if that buffer is freed or reallocated before the AST is consumed.
